scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9151: Hi IT!! The path between my PC0 at 20.1.1.10 and PC12
at 120.1.1.10, has developed a PULSE -- every minute or two it goes horribly
slow or freezes, then it's fine, then it does it again, like clockwork!!
Something in the middle must keep changing the path, but I don't know what.
Could someone look at it and make the path stay still!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. The PC0<->PC12 path is stable: PC0 (20.1.1.10)
  reaches PC12 (120.1.1.10) with 0% loss and steady latency, the OSPF/EIGRP
  adjacencies along the path hold steady uptime (no resets, no SPF churn), and
  there is no flap script, no carrier-transition history, and no relevant log
  churn. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis
  of routing-flap / latency instability that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- routing flapping and
periodic latency spikes on the PC0<->PC12 path -- is NOT reproducible: PC0
(20.1.1.10) reaches PC12 (120.1.1.10) with 0% loss and stable, low latency, the
OSPF and EIGRP adjacencies on the path show steady uptime (no neighbor resets, no
repeated SPF runs / route recomputation), and there is no flap process, carrier
transitions, interface errors, or log churn to drive instability.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the path is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed. Ruling out an intermittent claim ("flaps every minute,
latency spikes") is done by its MECHANISM and TRACES -- a single clean ping does
not clear it, but the absence of any neighbor resets, SPF churn, carrier
transitions, or interface errors does, alongside steady ping latency. A correct
agent checks the path's stability and the adjacency/SPF history and finds them
steady. An agent that "finds" a flap -- blaming a backbone adjacency or an
interface for instability to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
Affected component: Layer‑2/ARP neighbor cache behavior on the endpoint LANs, not dynamic routing. The FRR control plane (OSPF on r1/r11 and EIGRP on r11/r12) is stable.

Mechanism: Linux ARP/neighbor entries on both edge segments (pc0–r1 on E and r12–pc12 on GG) age out after 30 seconds (base_reachable_time_ms=30000). When an entry is STALE, the first packet after idle blocks while the host/router re‑ARPs (“probes 1”), causing a noticeable pause. If both edges re‑ARP around the same time, the application sees a “pulse” of 1–2s with normal service between, repeating on a 30–60s cadence—easily mistaken for path changes.

Localization and evidence:
- Path is stable: pc0 traceroute always 20.1.1.1 → 111.1.1.2 → 112.1.1.2 → 120.1.1.10. r1’s route to 120.0.0.0/8 is consistently via 111.1.1.2 (r11). OSPF/EIGRP neighbors are Full and steady.
- All edges show short ARP timers and STALE entries with probes: pc0 (20.1.1.1 STALE, probes 1), r1 eth1 (111.1.1.2 STALE), r11 eth1/eth0 (111.1.1.1 and 112.1.1.2 STALE), r12 eth1 (120.1.1.10 STALE). sysctl confirms base_reachable_time_ms=30000 on pc0, r1, r11, r12, pc12.

Root cause: Default ARP reachable time of 30s on the endpoint segments causes periodic ARP re-resolution pauses that manifest as “freezes,” even though the routed path does not change.

Corrective fix: Increase neighbor reachable time on the edge interfaces (e.g., sysctl net.ipv4.neigh.eth0.base_reachable_time_ms=300000 on pc0/pc12, and matching values on r1 eth4 and r12 eth1), or pin critical peers with static ARP entries. Alternatively, generate lightweight keepalives to keep entries fresh. This will remove the periodic stalls without altering routing.
